title: All Saints (1 November)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of the Rosary and a garden of prayers. Your line was the month of beads.

The Church's calendar is crowded with saints: apostles and martyrs, popes and peasants, page after page of names, each with a day. Yet behind those names, the Church believes, there's a crowd beyond counting. A farmer in a village nobody's heard of who prayed every morning of his life. A night nurse. A man who quietly forgave his brother. No statue, no day, no feast. So once a year the Church throws them all one party.
screen: `PAGE AFTER PAGE OF NAMES.` → `A CROWD BEYOND COUNTING.` → `ONE FEAST FOR ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: The feast grew from the martyrs. In the early centuries there were so many that no calendar could hold them, and Christians in the East began keeping one day for all martyrs together. In Rome, Pope Boniface IV took the Pantheon, the old temple to all the Roman gods, and dedicated it to Mary and all the martyrs. Later, Pope Gregory III dedicated a chapel at Saint Peter's to all the saints, and the first of November became the date, spreading across the West. The reading comes from Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne." Which no man could number. That's the point. In Catholic teaching, a saint isn't only someone the Church has formally canonized. Canonization says, with confidence, this person is in heaven and can be held up as an example. But everyone in heaven is a saint, and the Church assumes that's a huge crowd, most of them never named. The Gospel is the Beatitudes: blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers. Not a list of famous deeds; a description of ordinary people living a certain way. All Saints is a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation. And it opens a two-day pair: tomorrow, all who have died.
screen: `FIRST, ALL THE MARTYRS.` · `THE PANTHEON, FOR THE MARTYRS.` · `A MULTITUDE NO ONE COULD NUMBER.` · `MOST OF THEM NEVER NAMED.` · then, large: `A GREAT MULTITUDE, WHICH NO MAN COULD NUMBER.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind whose goodness nobody ever wrote down: a relative, a teacher, the woman who ran the parish soup kitchen, a neighbor who checked on everyone, living or dead. Picture their hands and what those hands did. If you pray, thank God for them, or ask their prayers, as Catholics do; if you don't, simply honor them in silence.
All Saints. The first of November, a feast for every saint in heaven, the known and the unknown, the multitude no one could number. Today's word.
Your line: the ones nobody knew. Most saints, Catholics believe, were never named. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate All Saints on 1 November as a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation, with the Beatitudes as the Gospel; in some parishes children dress as saints the evening before.

chat.says: Who counts on All Saints' Day? Only the famous saints?
options: Everyone in heaven, Catholics believe: a crowd no one could number, most of them never named.
Only the people the Church has formally canonized, the ones with their own feast days.
Only the early martyrs, since the feast started in Rome as their day alone.
chat.meaning: Canonization names some saints with confidence, but Catholics hold that everyone in heaven is a saint, most never named.

notes: Pantheon dedication by Boniface IV on 13 May 609 or 610; confirm.
Gregory III (731–741) chapel at Saint Peter's for all saints on 1 November; Gregory IV extended the feast more widely c. 835. Confirm.
'A few hundred names' on the General Roman Calendar is approximate; confirm.
Children dressing as saints on the eve: a modern parish custom in some places.
